title: Lost in Translation
full_review:
Two lonely Americans on business in Japanfind comfort and common ground amid the neon cacophony of Tokyoin the likable dramedy "Lost in Translation" (Focus).

Director Sofia Coppola, daughter of filmmaker Francis Ford Coppola, elicits nuanced performances in this ruminative meditation on loneliness and the emotional balm of friendship.

Reining in his comic shtick for reserved warmth, Bill Murray stars as Bob Harris, a fading movie star shooting a whiskey ad campaign in the land of the Rising Sun -- an event he gets to see regularly, thanks to a bout of insomnia brought on by a cocktail of jetlag and midlife anxiety. Bleary-eyed and unable to sleep, Harris trolls the posh hotel's piano bar. During one such late-night excursion he, in a chance encounter, meets fellow Yank Charlotte (Scarlett Johansson), a young newlywedwhose chronically absent photographer husband (Giovanni Ribisi) leaves her singing the culture-shock blues solo.

Their antennas tuned in to their mutual aloneness, the two lost souls immediately pick up each other's emotional distress signals. In addition to an American passport, they also discover that they have other things in common -- nocturnal restlessness and a realization that each is a stranger, not only in Japan, but in their own personal relationships.

Though forgetful of his kids' birthdays, Harris is a devoted father, yet he confides to Charlottethat the quotidian demands of parenthood have taken a toll on his marriage. At the opposite end of the marital spectrum, Charlotte, with the ink still wet on her wedding license, is struggling to get her bearings and find meaning in her life and new spousal identity.

Though separated in age by decades, the two snoozeless sake-mates spend a sleep-deprived week together, each supplying the missing pieces of the other's emotional jigsaw puzzle.

To its credit, the May-December friendship remains chaste, despite the characters' obvious attraction for each other. Harris' one sexual indiscretion -- not involving Charlotte-- is presented as a momentary moral lapse, a mistake that puts their friendship in jeopardy.

Less clear is the film's morally ambiguous ending, which leaves the door ajar for future infidelity.

Well crafted and acted, "Lost in Translation" strikes an appealing balance of poignant drama and lighthearted comedy, painting a tender and layered portrait of both physical and emotional isolation and effectively capturing the sense of being a stranger in a strange land.

In wisely remaining intimate in scope, Coppola has carpentered a narrative that touches on universal themes which resonate with viewers' shared need for interpersonal connection.

Thankfully, despite its title, little of this film's substance is lost in translation.

Due to some crude language and an implied sexual encounter, as well as a scene in a strip club with brief frontal nudity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
